Reproducing Peron et al. (2020) from CRCNS ssc-11¶

Paper. Peron S, Pancholi R, Voelcker B, Wittenbach JD, Olafsdottir HF, Freeman J, Svoboda K (2020). Recurrent interactions in local cortical circuits. Nature 579, 256-259. doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2062-x. The claims file (claims/peron-2020.yaml) was written from the version of record, with its Methods, Extended Data figure legends, Extended Data Table 1 and reporting summary.

Data set. CRCNS ssc-11 (doi:10.6080/K0Z31WWG), read from the public bucket crcnsarchive under ssc-11/live/data/, one an<id>.tar.gz per mouse (16 files, 120.9 GB compressed). CRCNS data sets are not versioned, so the version is recorded as unversioned; the bucket holds one copy of each file (no old/ folder), the one described by the data descriptor version 0.6 (20 February 2020), which is the version the paper's data statement points to. It is pinned here by the MD5 sums of checksums.md5, printed below for every file read, so that a later change is detectable.

Reading. A gzip stream cannot be read at an offset, so each archive is streamed once from front to back and every member the claims use is reduced in memory as it passes (helper peron2020.py). Nothing is written to disk. Four archives are read at a time; the full pass takes 11 to 18 minutes, depending on the connection (648 s in one run and 1,052 s in another; the time of this run is printed below).

Code. Methods the claims file does not fix are taken from the paper's analysis code, github.com/peronlab/ablation at commit 74b7321, which the claims file cites; each place is named in the helper's docstring or the cell that uses it.

Claim Tested here
model-amplification-increases, model-equal-connectivity-ablation-increases, model-increased-connectivity-ablation-decreases, model-more-ablation-larger-decline, model-slow-input-sensitive, model-response-similarity Yes: the network model of the Methods, rebuilt and simulated here (last sections)
model-all-or-none-robust No: the Methods' rule for its input strength gives no positive strength here (blocked, see its section)
neurons-per-mouse, representation-sizes Yes
touch-ablation-size, whisking-ablation-size, silent-ablation-size Yes
touch-ablation-reduces-touch, touch-ablation-touch-count, touch-ablation-whisking-unchanged Yes
whisking-ablation-no-effect-touch, whisking-ablation-no-effect-whisking Yes
silent-ablation-no-effect-touch, silent-ablation-no-effect-whisking Yes
ablation-type-specificity, ablation-size-correlation Yes

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import optimize, stats

import peron2020 as P

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)

started = time.time()
md5 = P.checksums()
data, sizes = P.load_all(workers=4)
print(f"CRCNS {P.DATASET}, version {P.VERSION} (doi:{P.DOI})")
print(f"streamed {len(data)} archives in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
for a in sorted(data):
    r = data[a]
    print(f"an{a}.tar.gz  md5 {md5['data/an' + a + '.tar.gz']}  {sizes[a] / 1e9:5.2f} GB  "
          f"read {r.get('bytes', 0) / 1e9:5.2f} GB in {r.get('seconds', 0):4.0f} s, reconnections {r.get('reopens')}, "
          f"errors {len(r['errors'])}")

Data check¶

What each archive holds, against the data descriptor ("session_neuropilone_????_merged" directories of an*_vol_NN_sess_struct.mat files, and ablation logs) and the paper (16 mice, 24 ablations, 4 to 6 subvolumes of 3 planes, imaging at about 7 Hz).

Duplicates. The analysis code reuses one directory as the post-ablation data of one ablation and the pre-ablation data of the next (get_data_path.m); that is by design. The check below looks for the same recording deposited twice: two session files, in any archive, with the same number of cells, frames and trials and identical touch scores.

fp = {}
for a in sorted(data):
    for dname, fl in data[a]["sess"].items():
        for fn, r in fl.items():
            t = r["per"]["t"]
            key = (len(r["ca_ids"]), r["n_frames"], r["n_trials"], np.round(np.nan_to_num(t[:50]), 6).tobytes())
            fp.setdefault(key, []).append(f"an{a}/{dname}/{fn}")
dups = [v for v in fp.values() if len(v) > 1]
print("Session files:", sum(len(v) for v in fp.values()), "; distinct recordings:", len(fp), "; duplicated groups:", len(dups))
for v in dups:
    print("  ", v)

Clocks. The encoding scores were computed by the authors; this attempt does not recompute them from dF/F. It checks that the touch times and the imaging frames share a clock: for each session file, the mean dF/F of that file's neurons with touch score above 0.1 is aligned to the first touch of each trial, and to the same times shifted 2 s earlier. A response that rises after the true touch times and not after the shifted ones shows the alignment.

In [5]:
rowc = []
for a in sorted(data):
    for dname, fl in data[a]["sess"].items():
        for fn, r in fl.items():
            lags = r["trig_lags"]
            base = lambda v: np.nanmean(v[(lags >= -5) & (lags <= -1)])
            resp = lambda v: np.nanmean(v[(lags >= 1) & (lags <= 6)])
            rowc.append({"mouse": a, "dir": dname, "file": fn, "n_onsets": r["trig_n"],
                         "true": resp(r["trig_real"]) - base(r["trig_real"]),
                         "shifted": resp(r["trig_shift"]) - base(r["trig_shift"])})
clk = pd.DataFrame(rowc)
print(f"Session files: {len(clk)}; response after true touch onsets (mean dF/F, frames 1 to 6 minus -5 to -1): "
      f"median {clk.true.median():.3f}, positive in {(clk.true > 0).sum()}")
print(f"Same for onsets shifted 2 s earlier: median {clk.shifted.median():.3f}, positive in {(clk.shifted > 0).sum()}")
print("Wilcoxon signed-rank, true against shifted, over files: p =", f"{stats.wilcoxon(clk.true, clk.shifted).pvalue:.2g}")
per_mouse = clk.groupby("mouse")[["true", "shifted"]].median().round(3)
print(per_mouse.T.to_string())
print("Files where the true response is not larger than the shifted one:")
print(clk[clk.true <= clk.shifted].to_string(index=False))
r0 = data["272761"]["sess"]["session_neuropilone_preablate_merged"]
r0 = r0[sorted(r0)[0]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
ax.plot(r0["trig_lags"], r0["trig_real"], label="first touch")
ax.plot(r0["trig_lags"], r0["trig_shift"], label="2 s earlier")
ax.set_xlabel("frames from onset"); ax.set_ylabel("mean dF/F, touch-scored cells"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("an272761 vol 1 pre")
print("Plotted range:", np.round([np.nanmin([r0['trig_real'], r0['trig_shift']]), np.nanmax([r0['trig_real'], r0['trig_shift']])], 3))

Per-neuron tables¶

For each of the 24 ablations, the table of get_ablation_data.m: pre-ablation and post-ablation touch and whisking scores, shuffle rejections, event rates, positions, the ablated neurons of the curation files, and the two proximity exclusions (the Methods cylinder, the main reading; the code's signed depth rule, a variant). Neurons are matched across periods by ROI id, as the code does; that a ROI id names the same neuron in the pre and post files is an assumption the data set does not let us check beyond the ids themselves (the session files are merged across days by the authors).

In [6]:
T, INFO = {}, {}

representation-sizes¶

Across 16 mice, 901 ± 539 of the imaged neurons encoded touch (fraction 0.108 ± 0.051) and 865 ± 364 encoded whisking (fraction 0.106 ± 0.028).

Readings of the criterion: (a) score above 0.1 alone in the first pre-ablation data (ablation_summ_stats.m); (b) the Methods membership rule in that period.

touch-ablation-size, whisking-ablation-size, silent-ablation-size¶

Touch ablations removed 16.8 ± 12.8 strong touch neurons per mouse (about 6% of the touch neurons of the barrel column, 9 mice), whose touch scores were at the 70th ± 35th percentile. Whisking ablations removed 12.7 ± 5.7 strong whisking neurons per mouse (about 4%, 7 mice), at the 66th ± 37th percentile of whisking score. Silent-neuron ablations (event rate below 0.025 Hz) removed 16.3 ± 2.6 neurons per mouse in 8 mice.

Two percentile rules, pooled over ablated neurons. The criterion's rule is a rank: the fraction of included neurons whose score is at or below the ablated neuron's (1 when none exceeds it; ablated neurons with no score are left out). The code's rule (ablation_summ_stats.m) is the position of the first included neuron whose score exceeds the ablated neuron's, over the number of included neurons; when none exceeds it, or the ablated neuron has no score, the position is the first, so the value is 1/N (the synthetic check below gives 0.01 for a score above all 100).

In [10]:
def pct(d, rank_r, own_r):
    """The code's rule (ablation_summ_stats.m): position of the first included neuron whose
    score exceeds the ablated neuron's, over the number included. When none exceeds it, or
    the ablated neuron's score is NaN, the position is the first one, so the value is 1/N."""
    ss = np.sort(d[f"{rank_r}_pre"][P.members(d, rank_r)].values)
    q = []
    for v in d[d.is_ablated == 1][f"{own_r}_pre"].values:
        ii = np.where(ss > v)[0]
        q.append((ii[0] + 1 if len(ii) else 1) / len(ss))
    return q

def pct_rank(d, rank_r, own_r):
    """The criterion's rule: rank of the ablated neuron's score among the included neurons'
    scores, as the fraction of them at or below it (1 when none exceeds it); NaN scores have
    no rank and are left out."""
    ss = np.sort(d[f"{rank_r}_pre"][P.members(d, rank_r)].values)
    v = d[d.is_ablated == 1][f"{own_r}_pre"].values
    v = v[~np.isnan(v)]
    return list(np.searchsorted(ss, v, side="right") / len(ss))

def above_all(d, rank_r, own_r):
    ss = d[f"{rank_r}_pre"][P.members(d, rank_r)].values
    v = d[d.is_ablated == 1][f"{own_r}_pre"].values
    return int((v > np.nanmax(ss)).sum()), int(np.isnan(v).sum()), len(v)

Result: touch-ablation-size partially reproduced. 16.78 ± 12.77 neurons per mouse and 5.85% of 287 are within tolerance. The percentile under the criterion's rule (the rank of each ablated neuron's score among the included touch neurons) is 79.3 ± 27.1 over the 145 ablated neurons with a score, outside 70 ± 7 and 35 ± 3.5. The code's rule gives 70.3 ± 35.0, the paper's values: it puts the 9 ablated neurons that score above every included neuron, and the 6 with no score, at 1/N in place of the top (the synthetic check gives 0.01 for a score above all 100). The paper's percentile is therefore that rule's, and the gap is asked of a reader.

Result: whisking-ablation-size partially reproduced. 12.71 ± 5.68 neurons are within tolerance; 4.43% of 287 is outside 4 ± 0.4. Under the criterion's rank rule the percentile is 75.4 ± 31.8 (Rwhisking among whisking neurons) or 75.8 ± 30.2 (among the touch neurons' Rtouch), both outside 66 ± 6.6; the code's rule gives 68.8 ± 36.2 and 65.9 ± 36.5, within tolerance.

Result: silent-ablation-size reproduced. 16.25 ± 2.55 neurons per mouse. Of the 130 ablated neurons, 118 have a pre-ablation event rate below 0.025 Hz in these data (the highest is 0.079 Hz). The paper gives the 0.025 Hz rule for choosing targets; 12 of the 130 ablated neurons are above it in these pre-ablation data.

Score changes by ablation type¶

The common method of the claims file: per mouse, the median pre and post score of the members of a representation; grand median across mice; Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired mouse medians. Counts of members per period follow touch-ablation-touch-count. The Methods cylinder is the main reading and the code's rule a variant.

In [11]:
def type_summary(abl, r, cyl="methods"):
    rows = []
    for a in P.ANIMS[abl]:
        d = P.with_cyl(T[(a, abl)], cyl)
        pre, post, n = P.mouse_medians(d, r)
        ca = P.class_counts(d, r, "a")
        cad = P.class_counts(d, r, "a", keep_ablated=False)
        cb = P.class_counts(d, r, "b")
        rows.append({"mouse": a, "pre": pre, "post": post, "change": post - pre, "n": n, "n_a_pre": ca[0], "n_a_post": ca[1],
                     "n_adrop_pre": cad[0], "n_adrop_post": cad[1], "n_b_pre": cb[0], "n_b_post": cb[1],
                     "score_ablated": float(np.nansum(d.t_pre[d.is_ablated == 1]))})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def show(abl, r):
    out = {}
    for cyl in ["methods", "code"]:
        s = type_summary(abl, r, cyl)
        p = stats.wilcoxon(s.pre, s.post).pvalue
        out[cyl] = (s, p)
        print(f"[{cyl} cylinder] {abl} ablation, {'Rtouch' if r == 't' else 'Rwhisking'}: grand median {s.pre.median():.3f} -> {s.post.median():.3f} "
              f"(adjusted MAD {P.adj_mad(s.pre):.3f}, {P.adj_mad(s.post):.3f}); neurons {s.n.sum()}; signed-rank p = {p:.3f}; "
              f"median change {s.change.median():+.4f}, mice with a decline {(s.change < 0).sum()} of {len(s)}")
    s = out["methods"][0]
    print(s.round(4).to_string(index=False))
    print(f"Counts, mean over mice: (a) score > 0.1, ablated kept {s.n_a_pre.mean():.1f} -> {s.n_a_post.mean():.1f}; "
          f"(a) ablated left out {s.n_adrop_pre.mean():.1f} -> {s.n_adrop_post.mean():.1f}; (b) Methods rule {s.n_b_pre.mean():.1f} -> {s.n_b_post.mean():.1f}")
    print(f"Sum over mice of the (a) pre-ablation count: {s.n_a_pre.sum()}")
    return out

R = {}

touch-ablation-reduces-touch, touch-ablation-touch-count¶

Ablating touch neurons reduced the touch-encoding score of the spared touch neurons, from 0.123 to 0.100 (grand median across 9 mice, 8,392 neurons). After touch ablation the number of touch neurons fell, from 932 ± 634 to 716 ± 469 (mean ± s.d. over 9 mice), ablated neurons excluded.

Result: touch-ablation-reduces-touch reproduced. Grand median Rtouch 0.123 -> 0.100, signed-rank p = 0.004 (all 9 mice decline), within tolerance under both cylinders. The criterion's members number 7,121 neurons (7,089 with the code's cylinder), against the paper's 8,392; 8,392 is the sum over the 9 mice of the pre-ablation count of neurons with score above 0.1 (reading (a) of the counts), which is 8,392 here, so the paper's neuron count is that sum, not the number of neurons entering the medians.

Result: touch-ablation-touch-count reproduced. Under reading (a) the mean count goes from 932.4 to 715.8 with ablated neurons kept (the code), and 918.3 to 712.6 with them left out (the text); both within tolerance. Reading (b) gives 623.7 -> 472.6.

Where the paper's grand medians for whisking and silent ablations come from: ablation_summ_stats.m fills one matrix of mouse medians, indexed by the ablation's position in the list of all 24 ablations (touch 1 to 9, silent 10 to 17, whisking 18 to 24), and takes the median over the whole matrix. It prints the whisking block before the silent rows are filled (they are zeros then), and the silent block when all 24 rows are filled. The cell below recomputes both, from this attempt's mouse medians.

In [18]:
order = [("touch", a) for a in P.ANIMS["touch"]] + [("silent", a) for a in P.ANIMS["silent"]] + [("whisking", a) for a in P.ANIMS["whisking"]]
for r, lab in [("t", "Rtouch"), ("w", "Rwhisking")]:
    M = np.array([P.mouse_medians(T[(a, abl)], r)[:2] for abl, a in order])
    Mz = M.copy(); Mz[9:17] = 0
    print(f"{lab}: median over all 24 ablations {np.median(M[:, 0]):.3f} -> {np.median(M[:, 1]):.3f}   "
          f"median with the 8 silent rows zero (whisking block) {np.median(Mz[:, 0]):.3f} -> {np.median(Mz[:, 1]):.3f}")
print("Paper: silent Rtouch 0.115 -> 0.107, Rwhisking 0.115 -> 0.114; whisking Rtouch 0.112 -> 0.095, Rwhisking 0.108 -> 0.107")

Rtouch: median over all 24 ablations 0.115 -> 0.107   median with the 8 silent rows zero (whisking block) 0.112 -> 0.096

Rwhisking: median over all 24 ablations 0.115 -> 0.113   median with the 8 silent rows zero (whisking block) 0.109 -> 0.107
Paper: silent Rtouch 0.115 -> 0.107, Rwhisking 0.115 -> 0.114; whisking Rtouch 0.112 -> 0.095, Rwhisking 0.108 -> 0.107
In [19]:
# the paper's +/- values against two definitions of the adjusted MAD: 1.4826 x median absolute
# deviation (used above), and 1.4826 x MATLAB's default mad (mean absolute deviation)
mean_mad = lambda x: 1.4826 * np.mean(np.abs(np.asarray(x) - np.mean(x)))
paper_pm = {("touch", "t"): (0.021, 0.037), ("touch", "w"): (0.013, 0.024), ("whisking", "t"): (0.081, 0.069),
            ("whisking", "w"): (0.076, 0.076), ("silent", "t"): (0.021, 0.023), ("silent", "w"): (0.014, 0.015)}
for (abl, r), (pp, pq) in paper_pm.items():
    s = R[(abl, r)]["methods"][0]
    print(f"{abl:8s} {'Rtouch' if r == 't' else 'Rwhisking':9s}: median-based {P.adj_mad(s.pre):.3f} / {P.adj_mad(s.post):.3f}; "
          f"mean-based {mean_mad(s.pre):.3f} / {mean_mad(s.post):.3f}; s.d. {s.pre.std(ddof=1):.3f} / {s.post.std(ddof=1):.3f}; paper {pp} / {pq}")
# the whisking and silent medians of the paper come from the 24-row matrix (cell above); the same matrix for the spread
for r in ["t", "w"]:
    M = np.array([P.mouse_medians(T[(a, abl)], r)[:2] for abl, a in order])
    Mz = M.copy(); Mz[9:17] = 0
    for lab, X in [("whisking block, 8 zero rows", Mz), ("all 24 rows", M)]:
        print(f"{'Rtouch' if r == 't' else 'Rwhisking'} {lab}: median-based {P.adj_mad(X[:, 0]):.3f} / {P.adj_mad(X[:, 1]):.3f}; "
              f"mean-based {mean_mad(X[:, 0]):.3f} / {mean_mad(X[:, 1]):.3f}")

The paper's ± values are reproduced by 1.4826 times the mean absolute deviation (MATLAB's mad with its default flag), not by the median absolute deviation the text names: touch ablation Rtouch 0.021 / 0.038 against 0.021 / 0.037, and Rwhisking 0.013 / 0.024, equal to the paper. For the whisking and silent ablations they match only on the same matrices as the paper's medians (whisking block with eight zero rows 0.081 / 0.070 and 0.076 / 0.076; all 24 rows 0.021 / 0.023 and 0.014 / 0.015). The ± values above (median-based) are therefore about half the paper's for the touch ablations (0.011 / 0.016 against 0.021 / 0.037), and about a tenth for the whisking ablations (Rtouch 0.008 / 0.009 against 0.081 / 0.069), whose paper values come from the zero-padded matrix.

Result: whisking-ablation-no-effect-touch reproduced. Signed-rank p = 0.109 (Rtouch 0.113 -> 0.106 over the 7 whisking ablation mice; 4,605 member neurons), no change at the 0.05 level. The paper's 0.112 -> 0.095 are reproduced by the code's median over a matrix with eight zero rows (0.112 -> 0.096), not by the median over the 7 mice; the post value 0.106 is outside the claim's tolerance (0.085 to 0.105), but the criterion of this claim of absence is the test. Counts 838.0 -> 898.9 (reading (a)), and the (a) pre counts sum to 5,866, the paper's neuron count.

Result: whisking-ablation-no-effect-whisking reproduced. Signed-rank p = 0.938 with the Methods cylinder and 0.812 with the code's (the paper's value). Rwhisking 0.114 -> 0.110 over the 7 mice; the paper's 0.108 -> 0.107 is again the zero-padded median (0.109 -> 0.107 here). Counts 880.1 -> 973.7; the (a) pre counts sum to 6,161.

Result: silent-ablation-no-effect-touch reproduced. Signed-rank p = 0.383; Rtouch 0.111 -> 0.113 over the 8 mice. The paper's 0.115 -> 0.107 equal the median over all 24 ablations. Counts 888.8 -> 925.8; the (a) pre counts sum to 7,110.

Result: silent-ablation-no-effect-whisking reproduced. Signed-rank p = 0.844; Rwhisking 0.114 -> 0.115 over the 8 mice (the paper's 0.115 -> 0.114 are close to the 24-ablation median, 0.115 -> 0.113). Counts 960.5 -> 904.4; the (a) pre counts sum to 7,684.

ablation-type-specificity¶

Touch ablations produced significantly different changes in Rtouch from whisking or silent ablations, while whisking and silent ablations did not differ; for Rwhisking no pair of ablation types differed.

Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the per-mouse changes. With 9, 8 and 7 mice MATLAB's ranksum uses its exact method; scipy's mannwhitneyu with method="exact" is the same test.

In [20]:
for cyl in ["methods", "code"]:
    for r, lab in [("t", "Rtouch"), ("w", "Rwhisking")]:
        ch = {abl: R[(abl, r)][cyl][0].change.values for abl in ["touch", "silent", "whisking"]}
        p = lambda x, y: stats.mannwhitneyu(ch[x], ch[y], method="exact").pvalue
        print(f"[{cyl}] change in {lab}: touch-silent p = {p('touch', 'silent'):.3f}, touch-whisking p = {p('touch', 'whisking'):.3f}, "
              f"whisking-silent p = {p('whisking', 'silent'):.3f};  median changes touch {np.median(ch['touch']):+.4f}, "
              f"silent {np.median(ch['silent']):+.4f}, whisking {np.median(ch['whisking']):+.4f}")
print("Paper: Rtouch 0.002, 0.042, 0.152; Rwhisking 0.743, 0.758, 1")
# where 0.031 and the paper's 0.042 part: the same test on the table's own per-mouse changes
ch_t = {abl: R[(abl, "t")]["code"][0].set_index("mouse").change for abl in ["touch", "whisking"]}
for abl in ["touch", "whisking"]:
    e = EDT1[EDT1.ablation == abl].set_index("mouse").dRtouch
    print(f"{abl}: change in Rtouch here (code cylinder) and in Extended Data Table 1, by mouse:",
          {a: (round(ch_t[abl][a], 3), e[a]) for a in e.index})
et, ew = EDT1[EDT1.ablation == "touch"].dRtouch.values, EDT1[EDT1.ablation == "whisking"].dRtouch.values
print(f"rank-sum on the table's values, touch against whisking: p = {stats.mannwhitneyu(et, ew, method='exact').pvalue:.3f}; "
      f"with ties (asymptotic, as MATLAB ranksum uses for ties): p = {stats.mannwhitneyu(et, ew, method='asymptotic').pvalue:.3f}")
allv = np.r_[ch_t["touch"].values, ch_t["whisking"].values]
rk = stats.rankdata(allv)
print("ranks here, touch:", rk[:9].astype(int).tolist(), "whisking:", rk[9:].astype(int).tolist())
rk_e = stats.rankdata(np.r_[et, ew])
print("ranks in the table, touch:", rk_e[:9].tolist(), "whisking:", rk_e[9:].tolist())

Result: reproduced. For Rtouch, touch-silent p = 0.002 and touch-whisking p = 0.031, while whisking-silent p = 0.152; for Rwhisking all three are above 0.05 (0.743, 0.837, 0.955 with the Methods cylinder; 0.743, 0.758, 1.000 with the code's, the paper's values). Only the touch-whisking value differs from the paper's (0.031 against 0.042). The same test on the table's own per-mouse changes gives 0.042: an278937's whisking-ablation change is -0.003 here and -0.006 in the table, which swaps its rank (13 here, 12 in the table) with an257220's touch ablation (12 here, 13 in the table).

ablation-size-correlation¶

The decline in the touch representation grew with the touch representation ablated, the change in Rtouch correlating with the net Rtouch ablated (R = -0.794 over all 24 ablations; R = -0.779 over the 9 touch ablations).

Result: reproduced. R = -0.790 over the 24 ablations (p = 4.4e-06) and R = -0.761 over the 9 touch ablations (p = 0.017), both within tolerance and significant (-0.797 and -0.781 with the code's cylinder). One mouse (an250220, 50 neurons ablated) carries much of the touch-ablation correlation.

distance-dependence-touch, distance-dependence-whisking-absent¶

After touch ablation, touch neurons 15-35 um from the nearest ablated neuron lost more Rtouch than those 115-135 um away (-0.132 against -0.056), and the effect decayed with distance with a length constant of 87 um. Touch ablation produced no distance-dependent change in the whisking representation (proximal 0.000, distal -0.023).

Readings: (a) the code's (per-mouse means for the paired test; median over all neurons pooled for the values); (b) per-mouse medians, grand median as the value. Length constant: fit of a exp(b d) to the cross-mouse mean of per-mouse mean changes in 25-um bins from 0 to 150 um.

In [22]:
def distance(r, cyl):
    pm, dm, pmed, dmed, allp, alld, byb = [], [], [], [], [], [], []
    bins = np.arange(0, 151, 25)
    for a in P.ANIMS["touch"]:
        d = P.with_cyl(T[(a, "touch")], cyl)
        m = P.members(d, r)
        dd = d.d_ablated_um[m].values
        ds = (d[f"{r}_post"] - d[f"{r}_pre"])[m].values
        px, di = (dd > 15) & (dd < 35), (dd > 115) & (dd < 135)
        pm.append(np.nanmean(ds[px])); dm.append(np.nanmean(ds[di]))
        pmed.append(np.nanmedian(ds[px])); dmed.append(np.nanmedian(ds[di]))
        allp += list(ds[px]); alld += list(ds[di])
        byb.append([np.nanmean(ds[(dd >= bins[i]) & (dd < bins[i + 1])]) for i in range(len(bins) - 1)])
    x = bins[:-1] + 12.5
    y = np.nanmean(np.array(byb), 0)
    popt, _ = optimize.curve_fit(lambda x, a, b: a * np.exp(b * x), x, y, p0=(y[0], -0.01), maxfev=20000)
    return dict(pm=pm, dm=dm, pmed=pmed, dmed=dmed, allp=allp, alld=alld, x=x, y=y, lam=abs(1 / popt[1]), byb=np.array(byb))

Result: distance-dependence-touch reproduced. Under reading (a), proximal -0.133 and distal -0.056 (-0.132 and -0.056 with the code's cylinder, the paper's values), signed-rank p = 0.012 (0.020), and the length constant is 87.3 um (87.6), all within tolerance. Under reading (b) the values are -0.103 and -0.019 with p = 0.359, which do not match; the claim holds under (a).

Result: distance-dependence-whisking-absent reproduced. Under the code's reading the proximal and distal whisking changes are -0.004 and -0.023 (0.000 and -0.023 with the code's cylinder) and the paired test gives p = 0.164 (0.129; the paper reads 0.098 from its figure), so no distance dependence at the 0.05 level. Per-mouse medians (variant) give p = 0.652.

behaviour-unchanged¶

Ablations did not change whisker movement or behaviour, so behaviour does not account for the decline of the touch representation; no mouse showed a significant change in whisker angle, angle at touch or curvature change at touch.

Per mouse and ablation, over all pre and all post session files: fraction correct (hits over hits and errors; trials without a lick are not scored, as the code sums the first four trial types) and touch bursts per trial. Touches are merged into bursts at a 50 ms interval; the toolbox method the code calls is not public, so a touch starting less than 50 ms after the previous touch of the trial ended is taken to join its burst (an assumption; it bears only on touches per trial). Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests per mouse on the samples (Methods), and on normalized histograms as the code does (variant).

In [23]:
brow = []
for (a, abl) in P.ABLATIONS:
    b = P.behaviour(data[a], a, abl)
    row = {"mouse": a, "ablation": abl, "fc_pre": b["pre"]["frac_correct"], "fc_post": b["post"]["frac_correct"],
           "tpt_pre": b["pre"]["touches_per_trial"], "tpt_post": b["post"]["touches_per_trial"],
           "trials_pre": b["pre"]["n_trials"], "trials_post": b["post"]["n_trials"]}
    for v, edges in [("theta", np.arange(-45.5, 91, 1)), ("theta_at_touch", np.arange(-45.5, 91, 1)), ("kappa_at_touch", np.arange(-0.0255, 0.026, 0.001))]:
        x, y = b["pre"][v], b["post"][v]
        x, y = x[~np.isnan(x)], y[~np.isnan(y)]
        k = stats.ks_2samp(x, y)
        row[f"KS_{v}_p"], row[f"KS_{v}_D"], row[f"n_{v}"] = k.pvalue, k.statistic, min(len(x), len(y))
        hx, hy = np.histogram(x, edges)[0], np.histogram(y, edges)[0]
        row[f"KShist_{v}_p"] = stats.ks_2samp(hx / hx.sum(), hy / hy.sum()).pvalue
        row[f"median_shift_{v}"] = np.median(y) - np.median(x)
    brow.append(row)
beh = pd.DataFrame(brow)

Result: not reproduced. With the paired signed-rank test the legend names, fraction correct rises after silent ablations (mean 0.697 -> 0.786, p = 0.008) and touches per trial rise after whisking ablations (p = 0.047); for touch ablations neither changes (p = 0.910 and 0.570). The KS tests on the samples find a difference in all 24 ablations for whisker angle and in 23 of 24 for angle and curvature at touch, with small effects (median D 0.085, 0.128 and 0.105), as the large samples make the test sensitive. The code's tests find nothing: the rank-sum tests give no p below 0.05, and equal the figure's values for fraction correct (0.863, 0.065, 0.710) and for whisking-ablation touches (0.620); for touches per trial after touch and silent ablations they give 0.796 and 0.645 against 0.666 and 0.721, as the burst rule here is assumed. The KS tests on normalized histograms give no p below 0.05. So the paper's statistics come from unpaired tests, not the paired ones its legend names. The part of the statement about touch ablations (no change in behaviour that could explain the touch decline) holds under every test run here. The trial types begin HitL, HitR, ErrL, ErrR in every file of both formats, so fraction correct is hits over hits and errors; the touch properties have one value per event edge in all 201 files, so taking every other value gives one per touch.

response-similarity-touch-ablation, response-similarity-example, response-similarity-whisking-ablation¶

After touch ablation, the change in Rtouch depended on response similarity to the ablated neurons; similar neurons declined and neurons with negative similarity increased, while the whisking representation showed no such dependence. In an example touch ablation mouse (272761), the slope is -0.44. Ablation of whisking neurons had no similarity-dependent effect on either representation.

Members with score above 0.25. Main reading: trial averages of correct left and right trials concatenated (Methods), Methods cylinder, a line fitted to the neurons' points per mouse, sign test on the slopes. Variants: the code's trial average (right trials only), the code's cylinder, and the code's fit to bin means.

            SIM[(abl, ta, a)] = P.similarity(data[a], T[(a, abl)], a, abl, ta)

def sim_summary(abl, r, ta, cyl):
    rows, bms = [], []
    for a in P.ANIMS[abl]:
        d = P.with_cyl(T[(a, abl)], cyl)
        c = SIM[(abl, ta, a)]
        m = P.members(d, r, 0.25) & ~np.isnan(c)
        ds = (d[f"{r}_post"] - d[f"{r}_pre"]).values
        s_pts, s_bin, bm, n, n_in = P.similarity_slopes(c[m], ds[m])
        rows.append({"mouse": a, "slope_points": s_pts, "slope_bins": s_bin, "n": n, "n_in_bins": n_in})
        bms.append(bm)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), np.array(bms)

Result: response-similarity-touch-ablation not reproduced. Under the claims file's method (both trial averages concatenated, a line through each mouse's neurons), 7 of 9 touch slopes are negative (sign test p = 0.180, not below 0.05), and the whisking slopes are positive in 8 of 9 (p = 0.039), a dependence the claim says is absent; the mean bin change is above 0 at negative similarity, as stated. The paper's numbers are reproduced only with the code's trial average, which keeps the right-trial average alone: then 8 of 9 touch slopes are negative (p = 0.039) with 2,768 neurons in bins (code cylinder, bin-mean fit), and the whisking slopes give p = 0.508 with 1,085 neurons, both exactly the paper's values.

Result: response-similarity-whisking-ablation reproduced. With the claim's method the sign tests give p = 1.000 for touch neurons (3 of 6 slopes negative) and p = 0.688 for whisking neurons (4 of 6), so no similarity dependence at the 0.05 level, with 1,624 and 889 neurons (within tolerance of 1,692 and 935). Only 6 of the 7 mice enter: the six pre-ablation files of an278939's whisking ablation (its post-silent directory) hold no trial-averaged dF/F, so no similarity can be computed there (they hold 27 features, of which psthHitLeftTrialsMatrix and psthHitRightTrialsMatrix, which no other file uses for this analysis; an278939 enters with 0 neurons). The code's bin-mean fit (variant) gives p = 0.031 for touch neurons with both trial averages, and the right-trial point fit also gives 0.031.

ablation-no-off-target-event-rate¶

Ablation of silent neurons did not change the calcium event rate of neurons adjacent (10-25 um) to the ablated cells (0.014 Hz before and after).

As ablation_figure_distance.m (event_rate_plot): neurons more than 10 and less than 25 um from the closest ablated neuron, leaving out ablated and cylinder-excluded neurons, all representations; per-mouse median event rate; signed-rank test.

In [30]:
for cyl in ["methods", "code"]:
    pre, post, n, per = [], [], 0, []
    for a in P.ANIMS["silent"]:
        d = T[(a, "silent")]
        ex = (d[f"prox_{cyl}"] == 1) | (d.is_ablated == 1)
        adj = (d.d_ablated_um > 10) & (d.d_ablated_um < 25) & ~ex
        pre.append(np.nanmedian(d.er_pre[adj])); post.append(np.nanmedian(d.er_post[adj])); n += int(adj.sum())
        per.append((a, int(adj.sum()), round(pre[-1], 4), round(post[-1], 4)))
    print(f"[{cyl}] grand median {np.median(pre):.4f} -> {np.median(post):.4f} Hz (adjusted MAD {P.adj_mad(pre):.4f}, {P.adj_mad(post):.4f}); "
          f"{n} neurons; signed-rank p = {stats.wilcoxon(pre, post).pvalue:.4f}; mice with a lower rate after: {int(np.sum(np.array(post) < np.array(pre)))} of 8")
    print("   per mouse (mouse, n, pre, post):", per)

ablation-success-rate¶

About two thirds of ablation attempts succeeded; 293 cells were ablated successfully in 22 sessions in 14 mice with complete logs.

Targets and successes from the curation files (NYU: per-attempt targets and success flags; JRC: attempted_ids and ablated_ids). The JRC ablation logs' target ids (la.ablatedId, as ablation_figure_energy.m reads them) are compared with attempted_ids.

Result: reproduced. Over the 23 ablations with a list of targets, 320 of 474 targeted neurons were ablated (0.675, within 0.667 ± 0.067). Leaving out the two mice the legend names, 300 neurons were ablated successfully in 22 ablations of 14 mice, within tolerance of 293; the legend also leaves out 7 other ablations it does not name, so this count cannot be matched exactly. In the NYU mice the 510 per-attempt logs are the attempts of the curation files: each mouse has as many logs as curation-file attempts over its ablations (for example 30 + 61 = 91 in an275798), and their target ids are the curation files' targets (the 279 NYU targets are distinct neurons, several attempted more than once).

per-mouse-table¶

Extended Data Table 1 lists, for each of the 24 ablations, the mouse's neuron count, the ablation type, the number ablated, the touch and whisking neuron counts and the change in median Rtouch and Rwhisking.

Counts match within 10%, changes within 0.005. The touch and whisking counts are compared under reading (a) of representation-sizes (score above 0.1, first pre-ablation data of the ablation), reading (b), and the members entering the medians (the union of the pre and post periods, as in get_restricted_neurons.m), with each cylinder. The cell count of a second ablation is the mouse's (the table gives it once).

Result: partially reproduced. Under the main reading (the Methods cylinder) 23 of 24 rows match in cell count, ablated count and both changes; in an275801's touch ablation the change in Rtouch is -0.071 against the table's -0.065. With the code's cylinder (variant) all 24 rows match. The table's touch and whisking counts are the members that enter the medians under the code's cylinder (21 and 22 of 24 rows equal, all within 10%), not the counts of reading (a) or (b) (10 and 1 rows within 10% for touch), so the table was made with the code's rule.

Network model claims¶

The model outputs were not deposited (claims file, data: elsewhere), so the network of the Methods ("Network model") is rebuilt here in numpy and numba (helper peron2020_model.py, whose docstring gives the source of every parameter). The paper used Brian2; this is a reimplementation of the same equations and parameters, not the paper's code.

What the Methods leave open, and the choice made for each (each an assumption, recorded in the attempt):

  • The size of the background PSP. The Methods give its frequencies (5,000 and 2,000 Hz) and say they were "selected so that the tonic firing rate of these populations were approximately 0.5 Hz for excitatory neurons and 10 Hz for inhibitory neurons". One PSP per population is set here to give those rates at Pconn 0.2 without stimulus (first cell below).
  • The sign of inhibitory PSPs: -1 mV ("All connections had the same strength, which was chosen so that the resulting post-synaptic potential (PSP) is 1 mV").
  • The stimulus amplitude is its peak current; its value comes from the readings of the claims file's opening comment, (a) fraction of excitatory neurons with score above 0.1 equal to 0.108, (b) smallest Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance to the pooled pre-ablation Rtouch of the touch ablation mice, (c) fraction equal to 0.17. Reading (b) sets a strength only where its smallest distance lies at a positive strength inside the sweep, which reaches down to no input.
  • Which neurons enter "all neurons that met the 0.1 encoding score criteria": excitatory neurons only (main) and all neurons of the network, inhibitory ones included (variant). The Methods match the input on the "distributions of excitatory neuron encoding scores", ablate "the 20 excitatory neurons with the highest encoding score", and the in vivo data the model stands for are of excitatory neurons (Ai162 x Slc17a7-IRES2-cre mice; Emx1-IRES-cre mice, whose mCherry marks "only ... nuclei of excitatory neurons"; Methods, Mice). The paper's counts for Fig. 3b (3,466 and 3,779 neurons above 0.25 over 30 networks) are also nearer the excitatory counts here than those of all neurons (model-response-similarity cell). An earlier revision of this notebook counted all neurons; the two outcomes that the change moves were reviewed in a third verification round, which agreed with both.
  • The repeated run after ablation uses the same background and initial state as the run before (Brian2's store and restore); the 0-ablation networks of Extended Data Fig. 4 therefore show no change.

Every network is seeded by its index (0 to 29), so each claim's numbers do not depend on the order of the cells.

Calibration of the input strength¶

Sweeps of the peak input current, two networks per strength (seeds 900 and 901), for the touch input (peak 10 ms) and the slow input (peak 50 ms), at Pconn 0.2 and 0.4. For each strength, the fraction of excitatory neurons with score above 0.1 and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the excitatory scores and the in vivo distribution (pre-ablation Rtouch of every neuron of the 9 touch ablation mice). Reading (a) interpolates linearly to the fraction 0.108, reading (c) to 0.17, and reading (b) takes the strength of the grid with the smallest distance, set only when that strength is positive and inside the grid. Each sweep starts at no input (strength 0), so that a minimum at the weakest strength tried can be told from one at no input.

In [34]:
SW = {(0.2, 10.0): [0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 300, 400], (0.4, 10.0): [0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50],
      (0.2, 50.0): [0, 25, 50, 70, 90, 110, 140, 200], (0.4, 50.0): [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15]}
sw_jobs = [dict(kind="pre_only", seeds=[900 + k], pconn=pc, strength=float(s), peak_ms=pk) for (pc, pk), ss in SW.items() for s in ss for k in range(2)]
sw = PM.run_jobs(sw_jobs)
invivo = np.concatenate([T[(a, "touch")].t_pre.dropna().values for a in P.ANIMS["touch"]])
print(f"In vivo reference: {len(invivo)} neurons, fraction above 0.1 {np.mean(invivo > 0.1):.3f}, median {np.median(invivo):.3f}, "
      f"range {invivo.min():.3f} to {invivo.max():.3f}, fraction exactly 0 {np.mean(invivo == 0):.3f}")
cal = []
for (pc, pk), ss in SW.items():
    for s in ss:
        ds = [d for d in sw if d["pconn"] == pc and d["peak"] == pk and d["strength"] == s]
        e = np.concatenate([d["pre"][:PM.NEXC] for d in ds])
        cal.append({"pconn": pc, "peak_ms": pk, "strength": s, "frac_exc_0.1": np.mean(e > 0.1), "frac_exc_zero": np.mean(e == 0), "frac_S_0.1": np.mean(np.concatenate([d["pre"][:PM.NS] for d in ds]) > 0.1),
                    "median_exc_above_0.1": np.median(e[e > 0.1]) if (e > 0.1).any() else np.nan, "KS": stats.ks_2samp(e, invivo).statistic,
                    "rate_exc_Hz": np.mean([d["rate_pre"][:PM.NEXC].mean() for d in ds]), "rate_inh_Hz": np.mean([d["rate_pre"][PM.NEXC:].mean() for d in ds])})
cal = pd.DataFrame(cal)
print(cal.round(3).to_string(index=False))

def cross(x, f, target):
    """First crossing of ``target`` by f(x), linear interpolation between grid points."""
    for i in range(1, len(x)):
        if f[i - 1] < target <= f[i]:
            return float(x[i - 1] + (target - f[i - 1]) * (x[i] - x[i - 1]) / (f[i] - f[i - 1]))
    return np.nan

STR = {}
for (pc, pk), g in cal.groupby(["pconn", "peak_ms"]):
    x, f = g.strength.values, g["frac_exc_0.1"].values
    STR[("a", pc, pk)] = cross(x, f, 0.108)
    STR[("c", pc, pk)] = cross(x, f, 0.17)
    k = int(np.argmin(g.KS.values))
    STR[("b", pc, pk)] = float(x[k]) if 0 < k < len(x) - 1 else np.nan  # a minimum at no input or at the strongest input sets none
    print(f"Pconn {pc}, peak {pk:.0f} ms: (a) {STR[('a', pc, pk)]:.1f}; (b) {STR[('b', pc, pk)]:.1f} (smallest KS {g.KS.min():.3f} at strength {x[k]:g}; "
          f"next smallest {np.sort(g.KS.values)[1]:.3f}); "
          f"(c) {STR[('c', pc, pk)]:.1f} (largest fraction reached {f.max():.3f})")
print("\nAmplification (inverse of the matched input strength, normalized to Pconn 0.2), touch input:")
AMP = {}
for rd in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    s2, s4 = STR[(rd, 0.2, 10.0)], STR[(rd, 0.4, 10.0)]
    AMP[rd] = s2 / s4
    print(f"  reading ({rd}): strength {s2:.1f} at Pconn 0.2 and {s4:.1f} at 0.4; amplification at 0.4 = {AMP[rd]:.2f}; "
          f"strength at 0.4 below that at 0.2: {s4 < s2 if not np.isnan(s2 + s4) else 'not set'}")
    for p in [0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.44]:
        sp = s2 + (p - 0.2) / 0.2 * (s4 - s2)
        print(f"     interpolated strength at Pconn {p}: {sp:.1f}" + (f", amplification {s2 / sp:.2f}" if sp > 0 else ", not positive"))

Ablation runs¶

For each reading whose strengths could be set, 30 networks (seeds 0 to 29) at Pconn 0.2 (the 20 strongest excitatory encoders ablated) and at Pconn 0.4 (0, 10, 20 and 50 ablated, Extended Data Fig. 4), with the touch input; and with the slow input at both Pconn, under (a) the touch input strength and (b) a strength set anew by the same rule from the slow-input sweep.

In [35]:
RUNS = {}
def ckey(pc, s, pk, sizes):
    return (pc, round(float(s), 3), pk, tuple(sizes))

conds = []
for rd in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    if np.isnan(STR[(rd, 0.2, 10.0)]) or np.isnan(STR[(rd, 0.4, 10.0)]):
        print(f"reading ({rd}): no strength, not run")
        continue
    conds += [ckey(0.2, STR[(rd, 0.2, 10.0)], 10.0, (20,)), ckey(0.4, STR[(rd, 0.4, 10.0)], 10.0, (0, 10, 20, 50))]
    for pc in [0.2, 0.4]:
        conds += [ckey(pc, STR[(rd, pc, 10.0)], 50.0, (20,))]
        if not np.isnan(STR[(rd, pc, 50.0)]):
            conds += [ckey(pc, STR[(rd, pc, 50.0)], 50.0, (20,))]
conds = list(dict.fromkeys(conds))
NNET = 30
jobs = [dict(kind="condition", seeds=[sd], pconn=c[0], strength=c[1], peak_ms=c[2], sizes=c[3], run_seed=sd,
             with_similarity=(c[2] == 10.0)) for c in conds for sd in range(NNET)]
t0 = time.time()
out = PM.run_jobs(jobs)
for i, c in enumerate(conds):
    RUNS[c] = out[NNET * i:NNET * (i + 1)]
print(f"{len(conds)} conditions, {len(jobs)} networks, {sum(1 + sum(s > 0 for s in c[3]) for c in conds) * NNET} runs of 20 s, {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
for c in conds:
    rs = RUNS[c]
    print(f"  Pconn {c[0]}, strength {c[1]}, peak {c[2]:.0f} ms, sizes {c[3]}: rates before ablation, excitatory {np.mean([d['rate_pre'][:PM.NEXC].mean() for d in rs]):.2f} Hz, "
          f"inhibitory {np.mean([d['rate_pre'][PM.NEXC:].mean() for d in rs]):.2f} Hz; fraction of excitatory neurons above 0.1 "
          f"{np.mean([np.mean(d['pre'][:PM.NEXC] > 0.1) for d in rs]):.3f}")

def summarize(c, size=20, pop="exc", thresh=0.1):
    e = pd.DataFrame(PM.effect(RUNS[c], size, thresh, pop))
    e["change"] = e.post - e.pre
    p = stats.wilcoxon(e.pre, e.post).pvalue if (e.change != 0).any() else np.nan
    return e, p

def report(c, label, size=20):
    res = {}
    for pop in ["exc", "all"]:
        e, p = summarize(c, size, pop)
        res[pop] = (e, p)
        print(f"{label}, {'all neurons (variant)' if pop == 'all' else 'excitatory only (main)'}: grand median {e.pre.median():.3f} -> {e.post.median():.3f} "
              f"(adjusted MAD {P.adj_mad(e.pre):.3f}, {P.adj_mad(e.post):.3f}); signed-rank p = {p:.2g}; networks with an increase "
              f"{(e.change > 0).sum()} of {len(e)}; neurons per network {e.n.median():.0f} (range {e.n.min()} to {e.n.max()})")
    return res

model-amplification-increases¶

In the L2/3 network model, the sensory input needed to match in vivo responses declines as subnetwork connectivity rises, so amplification (network output over input, normalized to Pconn 0.2) increases with subnetwork connectivity.

The matched strengths and amplification under each reading are printed in the calibration cell above.

Result: reproduced, resting on assumptions. Under calibration (a) the matched strength is 218.0 at Pconn 0.2 and 28.2 at 0.4, so normalized amplification at 0.4 is 7.74, and the strength at 0.4 is below that at 0.2. Reading (a) is weakly set at Pconn 0.2: the fraction above 0.1 moves only from 0.106 to 0.109 between strengths 200 and 225, with two networks per strength, which bears on how large the amplification is, not on its direction. Reading (b) sets no strength at Pconn 0.4: with the sweep extended down to no input, the smallest KS distance for the touch input is at strength 0 (0.514), and the distance hardly depends on the input (over the whole sweep, 0.514 to 0.582), because 0.66 to 0.75 of the model's excitatory neurons score exactly 0 at every strength while almost no in vivo neuron does (fraction 0.000 to three decimals). At Pconn 0.2 its minimum is at 75 (0.468, with 0.469 and 0.470 at 100 and 125). Reading (c), the fraction 0.17, cannot be met: the largest fraction of excitatory neurons above 0.1 in any sweep is 0.119, as nearly only the 200 input-recipient neurons (11.8% of the excitatory population) reach it. The claim holds under the one reading that sets both strengths. Amplification here is far larger than the paper's Fig. 1c.

model-equal-connectivity-ablation-increases, model-increased-connectivity-ablation-decreases¶

In networks with equal subnetwork connectivity (Pconn 0.2), ablating the strongest encoders raises the encoding scores of spared neurons, from 0.237 to 0.274, owing to reduced feedback inhibition. In networks with increased subnetwork connectivity (Pconn 0.4), ablation lowers the encoding scores of spared neurons, from 0.243 to 0.143, because amplification is reduced.

Result: model-equal-connectivity-ablation-increases partially reproduced, resting on assumptions. At Pconn 0.2 under calibration (a), the spared excitatory neurons (above 0.1 before or after, ablated ones left out) go from a grand median of 0.546 to 0.562 (signed-rank p = 1.9e-09, 30 of 30 networks increase), the claimed increase at p < 0.001, with both values far outside 0.237 ± 0.024 and 0.274 ± 0.027. Counting all neurons (variant), the scores fall, 0.287 to 0.279 (p = 6.3e-05, 4 of 30 increase), and 0.287 is outside tolerance. With excitatory neurons the effect is present and the values are not, which is partially reproduced, as for the Pconn 0.4 claim. The scores here run about 2.3 times the paper's, and the rise (+0.016, about 3%) is smaller than the paper's (+0.037, about 16%).

Result: model-increased-connectivity-ablation-decreases partially reproduced, resting on assumptions. At Pconn 0.4 ablation lowers the spared neurons' scores under both populations: 0.356 to 0.231 (excitatory, p = 3.9e-07, 4 of 30 increase) and 0.282 to 0.096 (all neurons, p = 1.9e-08). Neither gives both grand medians within 0.243 ± 0.024 and 0.143 ± 0.014.

model-all-or-none-robust¶

Subnetwork connectivity above 0.4 gives all-or-none responses, a transient input driving the subnetwork into persistent activity, and such networks keep their all-or-none response after ablation of 10% of the subnetwork.

The criterion sets the input at Pconn 0.44 to twice the strength extrapolated from the two matched ones (Methods). The extrapolated strengths are printed in the calibration cell above.

Result: not tested (blocked, methods underspecified). Linear extrapolation of the two matched strengths to Pconn 0.44 gives -9.8 under calibration (a), and readings (b) and (c) set no strength at Pconn 0.4, so twice the extrapolated strength, the input the Methods use in this regime, is not a positive current here. The negative value follows from this attempt's calibration, whose amplification at Pconn 0.4 (7.7) is far above the paper's Fig. 1c. The Methods also give neither the matched strengths nor the strength and length of the reset pulse to the inhibitory population, and the pulse they place 300 ms after each onset falls on the next onset at the 300 ms interval of the claims file. No run was made.

model-more-ablation-larger-decline¶

In the model with Pconn 0.4, ablating more neurons (top 10, 20 or 50 encoders) gives larger declines in encoding score, the change correlating with the net encoding score ablated (R = -0.65).

In [37]:
for rd in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    if (rd, 0.4) not in MODEL:
        continue
    c = ckey(0.4, STR[(rd, 0.4, 10.0)], 10.0, (0, 10, 20, 50))
    for pop in ["exc", "all"]:
        rows = []
        for size in (0, 10, 20, 50):
            e, _ = summarize(c, size, pop)
            rows.append(e.assign(size=size))
        a_ = pd.concat(rows)
        med = a_.groupby("size").change.median()
        for lab, sub in [("with the 0-ablation networks", a_), ("without them", a_[a_["size"] > 0])]:
            sub = sub.dropna(subset=["change"])  # networks with no spared neuron above 0.1 have no median
            r_ = stats.pearsonr(sub.net_ablated, sub.change)
            print(f"reading ({rd}), {'all neurons (variant)' if pop == 'all' else 'excitatory only (main)'}, {lab}: R = {r_.statistic:+.3f}, p = {r_.pvalue:.2g}, n = {len(sub)}")
        print(f"   median change by size {med.round(4).to_dict()}; more negative at each larger size: {bool(np.all(np.diff(med.values) < 0))}; "
              f"median net score ablated by size {a_.groupby('size').net_ablated.median().round(2).to_dict()}")
print("Paper: R = -0.65, P < 0.01")

Paper: R = -0.65, P < 0.01

Result: model-more-ablation-larger-decline reproduced, resting on assumptions. Under calibration (a), with excitatory neurons, the median change falls with each larger ablation (0, -0.026, -0.123 and -0.209 for 0, 10, 20 and 50 ablated), and the change correlates with the net score ablated, R = -0.590 with the 0-ablation networks (p = 1.3e-12, n = 120), within -0.65 ± 0.065, and -0.456 without them (p = 6.3e-06). The criterion asks for R within tolerance under one of the two readings and a larger decline at each size, so it is met. With all neurons (variant) R is -0.726 and -0.558, both outside the tolerance. The margin is small: -0.590 is 0.005 inside the bound of -0.585, with fixed seeds. The outcome rests on two choices, the counted population and the inclusion of the 0-ablation networks, which the criterion leaves open; their 30 points sit at (0, 0), as the run after ablation repeats the same noise, and anchor the correlation. Calibration (b) gave the runs of the earlier revision (R = -0.774 and -0.678 with all neurons); with its sweep extended to no input it sets no strength at Pconn 0.4 (calibration cell), so it is not run.

model-slow-input-sensitive¶

Networks with Pconn 0.4 given slower, whisking-like input (peak at 50 ms) are also sensitive to ablation, encoding scores falling from 0.143 to 0.104; with equal subnetwork connectivity (Pconn 0.2) the slow-input representation is not degraded.

Result: model-slow-input-sensitive partially reproduced, resting on assumptions. With the slow-input strength set anew under calibration (a) (6.6 at Pconn 0.4, 87.3 at 0.2), the score of the excitatory neurons at Pconn 0.4 falls from 0.314 to 0.104 (p = 3.9e-07, 3 of 30 networks increase); the post value is within 0.104 ± 0.010 and the pre value is outside 0.143 ± 0.014. At Pconn 0.2 it rises, 0.803 to 0.850 (p = 1.9e-09, 30 of 30), so it is not degraded, as the claim says. With the touch-input strength (slow reading (a)) the score does not fall at Pconn 0.4 (0.952 to 0.947, p = 0.16). All neurons (variant) give 0.269 to 0.088 at Pconn 0.4 and no change at 0.2 (0.424 to 0.424, p = 0.21) with the strength set anew. No reading gives both grand medians within tolerance, so the effect is present and the values are not. Calibration (b) sets no strength for the slow input at Pconn 0.4 (calibration cell).

model-response-similarity¶

In networks with increased subnetwork connectivity, neurons whose activity is more similar to the mean activity of the ablated neurons lose the most encoding score after ablation; with equal connectivity the relationship is absent.

Neurons with score above 0.25 before or after ablation (ablated neurons left out); per network, a line through the neurons' change in score against their similarity to the mean rate of the 20 ablated neurons in the run before ablation (Methods), and a line through the means of 0.1-wide similarity bins as a variant (similarity_slopes of the data analysis).

In [39]:

    if np.isnan(STR[(rd, 0.2, 10.0)]) or np.isnan(STR[(rd, 0.4, 10.0)]):
        continue
    for pc, sizes in [(0.2, (20,)), (0.4, (0, 10, 20, 50))]:
        rs = RUNS[ckey(pc, STR[(rd, pc, 10.0)], 10.0, sizes)]
        for pop in ["exc", "all"]:
            sp, sb, n_ = [], [], 0
            for d in rs:
                m = PM.spared(d, 20, 0.25, pop)
                x, y = d["sim"][20][m], (d["post"][20] - d["pre"])[m]
                a1, a2, _, n1, _ = P.similarity_slopes(x, y)
                sp.append(a1); sb.append(a2); n_ += n1
            sp, sb = np.array(sp), np.array(sb)

                  f"negative, median slope {np.nanmedian(sp):+.3f}, sign p = {P.sign_test(sp):.2g}; bin-mean fit {np.sum(sb < 0)}/{np.sum(~np.isnan(sb))} negative, "

Result: model-response-similarity not reproduced, resting on assumptions. Under calibration (a), with excitatory neurons, the per-network slopes of the change in score against response similarity are negative at Pconn 0.2 (30 of 30, sign test p = 1.9e-09) and show no dependence at Pconn 0.4 (11 of 30 negative, p = 0.2), the reverse of the claim, which needs negative slopes at 0.4 and none at 0.2. All neurons (variant) give positive slopes at Pconn 0.4 (6 of 30 negative, p = 0.0014) and mostly positive ones at 0.2 (8 of 30 negative, p = 0.016). The bin-mean fit leans the same way. The excitatory counts (4,327 at Pconn 0.2 and 4,058 at 0.4) are nearer the paper's 3,779 and 3,466 than the counts of all neurons (7,815 and 7,078).

What the model section shows¶

The rebuilt network reproduces the direction of the paper's results at increased connectivity (amplification grows with Pconn; ablation lowers scores at Pconn 0.4, more for larger ablations, for touch and for slow input) and, with excitatory neurons counted, the rise in scores at equal connectivity, but not the paper's numbers, nor the response-similarity result. The choices the outcomes rest on are those listed at the top of the section (background PSP, inhibitory PSP, stimulus amplitude, which neurons are counted) and the calibration: (a) is the only reading that sets both matched strengths, as (b)'s smallest distance lies at no input at Pconn 0.4 and (c) cannot be met. Under the calibration the background gives 0.51 Hz and 10.35 Hz without stimulus, as the Methods ask, but at Pconn 0.4 the stimulus raises the excitatory rate to 2.78 Hz. The median score of the excitatory neurons above 0.1 is 0.553 at strength 200 and 0.578 at 225 (calibration sweep, Pconn 0.2), and the grand median of the spared excitatory neurons is 0.546, about 2.3 times the paper's 0.237. A failure here may be a failure of this reimplementation, not of the paper's model.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The encoding scores, shuffle scores, event rates and trial averages are the authors' own, read from the session files; nothing is recomputed from fluorescence. The Methods cylinder (|dz| < 30 um) is the main reading and the code's signed rule a variant; outcomes are the same under both except per-mouse-table (23 of 24 rows match under the Methods cylinder, 24 of 24 under the code's rule). Touch bursts are merged by an assumed rule (the toolbox method is not public). The paper's ± values are 1.4826 times the mean absolute deviation, not the median absolute deviation the text names. The network model is a reimplementation of the Methods in numpy and numba, with the background PSP, the sign of inhibitory PSPs, the stimulus amplitude and the counted population (excitatory neurons) chosen as stated in its section; its outcomes rest on those choices. The counted population was revised after the second verification round, and the two model outcomes it moves were agreed in a third.

What was found about the data set. All 16 archives (24 ablations) are there and readable; neuron counts and ablated counts equal Extended Data Table 1 in all 24 rows, and the per-ablation score changes match it within 0.005 in 23 of 24 rows under the Methods cylinder (several differ by 0.001 to 0.002; all 24 match with the code's cylinder). The session files come in two MATLAB formats (v5 and v7.3) with no note of it. The data descriptor names no file other than the session structs and the ablation logs; the curation files that say which neurons were ablated, and their two layouts (NYU per-attempt flags, JRC id lists), can only be found through the paper's code, and an250220's curation file lists no attempted neurons. an278937's pre-ablation directory has a sixth subvolume (995 neurons) with no post-ablation counterpart, and an278939's post-silent files lack the trial-averaged dF/F. No file in the archives holds histology. The paper's grand medians for whisking and silent ablations and its behaviour P values follow its code, which differs from what the text and legends describe.
